airport: large airport facilities with broad paved aviation areas and terminal-like structures, distinguishing airport from farmland by lacking cultivated parcel texture, from port by lacking shoreline docks and harbor-water context, and from railwaystation by lacking concentrated rail-line organization.
bareland: broad exposed ground with barren surface and little vegetation, distinguishing bareland from desert by showing less homogeneous sand texture, from baseballfield by lacking sports-field geometry, and from farmland by lacking regular cultivated parcel boundaries.
baseballfield: compact sports field with a clear baseball-diamond layout and central infield geometry, distinguishing baseballfield from playground by stronger baseball-field structure, from pond by lacking water, and from bareland by lacking barren exposed-ground texture.
beach: bright shoreline region with clear sand-water boundary and coastal texture, distinguishing beach from resort by weaker built leisure infrastructure, from pond by broader coastal shoreline scale, and from port by lacking dock-side transport organization.
bridge: narrow man-made crossing structure spanning water or land, distinguishing bridge from pond by being a crossing rather than a compact water body, from viaduct by a more localized crossing form, and from port by lacking harbor-side logistics infrastructure.
center: dense urban core with concentrated buildings and organized city-block layout, distinguishing center from stadium by lacking a dominant sports field, from church by weaker single-landmark emphasis, and from parking by stronger surrounding built-up structure rather than open paved vehicle space.
church: prominent religious building or complex with distinctive landmark-like architecture, distinguishing church from square by stronger building dominance, from commercial by weaker business-block organization, and from center by emphasizing a single landmark structure rather than a broader urban core.
commercial: organized business district with dense building blocks and road access, distinguishing commercial from church by lacking landmark-like religious structure, from square by stronger building dominance, and from industrial by lacking heavy factory compounds and storage yards.
denseresidential: tightly packed residential roofs with very high housing density and minimal spacing, distinguishing denseresidential from mediumresidential by much closer building intervals, from sparseresidential by a far denser neighborhood texture, and from square by stronger repeated housing-roof structure rather than an open civic space.
desert: wide dry barren region with homogeneous arid texture and very little vegetation, distinguishing desert from mountain by weaker terrain relief, from pond by lacking water, and from bareland by stronger sand-like continuity.
farmland: regular cultivated land with visible parcel boundaries and agricultural texture, distinguishing farmland from meadow by stronger man-made plot organization, from airport by lacking broad paved aviation surfaces, and from industrial by lacking factory compounds and storage infrastructure.
forest: dense continuous tree canopy with natural dark-green texture, distinguishing forest from meadow by stronger canopy continuity, from mountain by weaker terrain relief, and from pond by lacking a central water body.
industrial: large factory-like compounds with utilitarian structures, storage yards, and production-oriented layouts, distinguishing industrial from storagetanks by not being dominated only by circular tank clusters, from railwaystation by weaker rail-line concentration, and from farmland by lacking cultivated parcel texture.
meadow: broad natural grass-covered open area with soft vegetation texture and weak structural boundaries, distinguishing meadow from farmland by lacking regular cultivated parcel boundaries, from forest by lacking dense continuous canopy, and from baseballfield by lacking formal sports-field geometry.
mediumresidential: moderately spaced residential buildings with visible yards and balanced housing density, distinguishing mediumresidential from denseresidential by larger spacing between houses, from resort by more regular residential neighborhood structure, and from sparseresidential by denser neighborhood grouping.
mountain: rugged elevated terrain with strong relief, slope shadows, and irregular topographic texture, distinguishing mountain from desert by stronger terrain variation, from forest by more obvious relief, and from pond by lacking a compact water body.
park: planned green open space with vegetation and leisure-oriented layout, distinguishing park from resort by weaker accommodation-like built structure, from square by stronger vegetation presence, and from pond by being land-dominant rather than water-dominant.
parking: large open paved area with organized parking rows and vehicle-oriented layout, distinguishing parking from viaduct by lacking elevated crossing structure, from commercial by weaker building dominance, and from center by lacking dense urban-core building blocks.
playground: recreational activity area with sports or play surfaces and open activity layout, distinguishing playground from baseballfield by lacking a baseball-diamond infield, from stadium by weaker venue enclosure, and from park by showing more explicit play-ground geometry.
pond: small enclosed water body with compact shape and visible boundary, distinguishing pond from bridge by being water rather than a crossing structure, from desert by clear water appearance, and from resort by lacking leisure-oriented built layout.
port: waterfront transport area with docks, vessels, and harbor-side logistics infrastructure, distinguishing port from resort by stronger transport and dock organization, from airport by shoreline-water context instead of aviation pavement, and from bridge by lacking a simple crossing structure.
railwaystation: transport hub with concentrated rail lines and station-related structures, distinguishing railwaystation from industrial by clearer rail-line concentration, from viaduct by lacking a simple elevated crossing form, and from airport by lacking broad aviation runways.
resort: leisure-oriented built environment with organized open spaces and accommodation-like structures, distinguishing resort from port by weaker dock-industrial structure, from park by stronger built tourism layout, and from beach by more visible built leisure organization beyond the shoreline.
river: elongated natural watercourse with continuous winding channel and visible banks, distinguishing river from pond by stronger linear flow shape, from desert by clear water dominance, and from farmland by lacking regular cultivated parcel boundaries.
school: campus-like area with multiple institutional buildings, open grounds, and organized educational layout, distinguishing school from square by stronger campus structure, from resort by weaker leisure-oriented organization, and from industrial by more educational-campus layout rather than factory compounds.
sparseresidential: widely separated residential houses with large open gaps and low housing density, distinguishing sparseresidential from resort by more regular neighborhood housing layout, from denseresidential by far lower roof density, and from church by lacking a single landmark-like dominant building.
square: open civic plaza-like space embedded in urban area, distinguishing square from church by weaker landmark-building dominance, from park by less vegetation, and from commercial by more central open-space structure and less dense building coverage.
stadium: large sports complex with prominent field and stronger enclosure or spectator-related structure, distinguishing stadium from playground by more venue-like framing, from center by emphasizing a dedicated sports facility, and from school by stronger field-centered sports organization.
storagetanks: clusters of large circular industrial tanks with highly regular round geometry, distinguishing storagetanks from industrial by stronger circular-container dominance, from port by weaker dock-water context, and from farmland by lacking cultivated parcel texture.
viaduct: elongated elevated transport structure with clear grade-separated linear form, distinguishing viaduct from bridge by a more extended raised-traffic pattern, from parking by lacking flat vehicle rows, and from railwaystation by lacking concentrated station-like rail organization.
